topic: Why your top spenders query missed your actual best customer using sql (written for a complete beginner with no prior knowledge; mostly watching, minimal hands-on requirement)

market_analysis.why_now: SQL content is exploding on short-form platforms as data literacy becomes a baseline expectation for marketing, product, and business roles. The counterintuitive angle of a simple query being WRONG hooks the growing audience of people learning SQL who assume SELECT and ORDER BY are all they need.
market_analysis.target_learner: A complete beginner who has seen or written a basic SELECT query and thinks sorting by total spend is enough to find the best customer — likely a marketer, junior analyst, or career-switcher scrolling TikTok or Reels for bite-sized SQL knowledge.
market_analysis.learner_goal: Understand that a naive ORDER BY total_spent query can miss a loyal, frequent, recent customer who is actually more valuable — and see the one-line fix that reveals them.
market_analysis.competition_gap: Most SQL shorts teach syntax in a vacuum. Almost none show a real business scenario where a correct query gives a misleading answer. This video weaponizes surprise — the viewer feels smart, then gets humbled, then gets the fix, all in under two minutes.
market_analysis.platform_fit: TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts — the controversial hot-take format (your query is WRONG) performs extremely well in short-form feeds where pattern interrupts drive watch-through rates.

content_structure.hook: This SQL query finds your top spender. It also completely misses your best customer. Let me show you why.
content_structure.core_promise: You will see exactly how a simple ORDER BY total_spent query hides a more valuable customer and learn the one tweak that reveals them.

lessons.title: The top spender query lied to you — here is the customer it buried
lessons.learning_objective: By the end of this lesson the learner will be able to explain why sorting customers by total spend alone can hide a more valuable customer and recognize that factoring in recency or frequency changes the answer.

scenes.scene_title: The query that looks right but is not
scenes.what_learner_sees: A simple customers table with five rows: name, total_spent, last_order_date, order_count. The presenter runs SELECT name, total_spent FROM customers ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1. Result: Big Corp at $48,000. Then the presenter scrolls to reveal the full table — a customer named Sara with $12,000 total but 47 orders in the last 90 days, versus Big Corp with 1 order from 2 years ago.
scenes.what_learner_hears: Here is your classic top spender query. Big Corp wins with 48 grand. Ship them a gift basket, right? But scroll down. Sara spent less overall — except she ordered 47 times in the last three months. Big Corp ordered once, two years ago, and ghosted you. Your top spender is a ghost. Sara is your actual best customer.
scenes.transition_to_next: Quick beat — so what do you do instead?

scenes.scene_title: The one-line fix that changes everything
scenes.what_learner_sees: The presenter modifies the query to add a WHERE clause: WHERE last_order_date >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) and changes ORDER BY to order_count DESC. Runs it. Sara now appears at the top. Big Corp is gone. A final text overlay says: Top spender is not the same as best customer. Filter by recency. Sort by frequency. Know the difference.
scenes.what_learner_hears: Add one WHERE clause — only customers who ordered in the last 90 days. Now sort by order count. Sara jumps to number one. Big Corp disappears. Total spend is a vanity metric without recency and frequency. One line of SQL just saved your marketing budget. Do not send the gift basket to a ghost.

lessons.key_takeaway: Sorting by total spend alone is a vanity metric — filtering by recency and sorting by frequency reveals who is actually driving your business right now.

exercise_file_plan.purpose: Contains the CREATE TABLE statement, sample data for five customers, the naive top-spender query, and the improved recency-plus-frequency query so curious viewers can paste it into any free SQL playground and try it themselves.

production_notes.hands_on_ratio: 5% — this is a watch-and-absorb format with an optional SQL file linked in bio for anyone who wants to try it
